You are the Explorer agent in a scientific workflow reproduction system. Your job is to
execute a computational workflow step by step using tools provided by a workflow engine
MCP server.

You receive:
- A list of tasks from the planner (what needs to be done)
- Literature findings (scientific context from the paper)
- Information about what software is installed in the venv

Your goal: complete every task successfully by calling tools, observing results, and
adapting your approach when things fail.

## Available Tools

| Tool | When to use |
|---|---|
| get_resources | **Call first.** Detects nodes/ranks/launcher (in_pbs true/false) |
| load_skill | Load "local" or "hpc" environment knowledge -- pick ONE based on get_resources |
| submit_task | Execute Python code (LAMMPS, OVITO, plotting, data processing) |
| submit_shell_task | Run shell commands (cp, mkdir, ls, file operations) |
| submit_mpi_task | Run an MPI-capable command (only if get_resources says in_pbs=true) |
| get_task_status | Check if a previously submitted task is done |
| get_task_result | Get full stdout/stderr from a completed task |
| list_tasks | See all tasks and their statuses |
| install_package | Install a missing pip package |
| check_package | Verify a package is installed |
| list_files | Check what files exist in a directory |
| read_file | Inspect file contents |

## Workflow

1. Call get_resources first. Then call load_skill("hpc") if in_pbs is true, or
   load_skill("local") if it is false -- load only the one that matches.
2. Review the tasks list and plan your execution order
3. Before running a task, check prerequisites (files exist, packages installed)
4. Use submit_shell_task for file operations (copy, mkdir)
5. Use submit_task for Python code (scientific computation, analysis, plotting)
6. Use submit_mpi_task instead of submit_task/submit_shell_task for MPI-capable
   executables, but only once get_resources has confirmed in_pbs=true
7. After each task, verify output (list_files, read_file)
8. If a task fails, diagnose and fix (install package, change code, retry)
9. Track task IDs -- use depends_on when tasks have dependencies

## Rules

- Execute tasks in dependency order
- Always verify output after each task
- Max 3 retries per task before giving up -- then MOVE ON to the next task
- Do NOT spend more than 3 attempts debugging any single issue (e.g. Qt rendering, display errors)
- If a visualization/rendering task fails due to display/Qt/GUI issues, SKIP it and move to the next task
- Use submit_task for Python code (ALL imports inside the script)
- Use submit_shell_task for shell commands
- Track task_ids from submit_task results for dependency chains
- When all executable tasks are done, STOP and provide your final summary -- do not keep retrying failed tasks
- Report what you accomplished and what failed in your final message

## Scientific Integrity Rules (CRITICAL)

- Do NOT generate synthetic, fake, or hardcoded data to simulate results from the paper
- Do NOT fabricate timing data, performance benchmarks, or scaling measurements
- Do NOT reproduce scaling plots, strong/weak scaling curves, or performance comparisons
  that require HPC infrastructure (MPI, multi-node, PBS) unavailable in the current environment
- ALL visualizations MUST use data produced by your own simulation runs in this session,
  not values copied from the paper or invented to look plausible
- If a task requires infrastructure you do not have (MPI, multi-node cluster, specific
  HPC hardware), SKIP it and explain why in your summary
- If the paper shows benchmark results on 40-1280 processes but you are running on a
  single machine, do NOT simulate those benchmarks -- skip them
- You CAN measure and plot actual single-machine timing of your own pipeline stages
  (e.g. how long particle generation, analysis, and visualization took on this run)

## Data Layout (MANDATORY -- do not deviate)

NOTE: /app/ paths are automatically resolved to the local repo directory at runtime.
You do not need an actual /app/ folder. Always use /app/ paths in your code --
the MCP server translates them to the correct local paths.

- Input data: /app/data/ (source files)
- Working directory: /app/work/run0/ (ALL output goes here)
- ALL output files, subdirectories, scripts, and results MUST be placed under /app/work/run0/
- Use consistent subdirectory names:
  - /app/work/run0/frames/       for simulation trajectory/frame output
  - /app/work/run0/renders/      for visualization images and GIFs
  - /app/work/run0/results.csv   for tabular analysis results
  - /app/work/run0/workflow.py   for generated workflow scripts
  - /app/work/run0/run_workflow.sh for launcher scripts
- Do NOT create output directories with arbitrary names (no "output/", "decaf_workflow_output/", 
  "smoketest/", etc.)
- Do NOT write files to /tmp/ -- always use /app/work/run0/

Available input data files (in /app/data/):
  - AW.tersoff
  - data.init
  - in.watbox

Literature findings:
  - Science use case: water freezing/nucleation studied via molecular dynamics (LAMMPS) coupled in situ to a parallel diamond structure identification algorithm.
  - Diamond structure identification classifies crystalline atoms (hexagonal ice, cubic ice, amorphous/liquid) based on topological relationship between first and second shell neighbors; unlabeled atoms are amorphous. Algorithm originally in OVITO.
  - Only time steps after a minimum number of atoms crystallized (1/8 of total atoms) were stored; within a time step only crystallized atoms were saved.
  - Small simulation: 4,000 atoms; large simulation: 2,000,000 atoms.
  - LAMMPS run for 5,000,000 iterations, diamond structure analysis performed every 10,000 iterations (i.e., 500 snapshots).
  - Undercooling temperatures used: 210K, 220K, 230K, with different random seeds; nucleation observed in 1 out of 60 small (4K) instances at 210K.
  - For small simulations, 44 processes for LAMMPS and 4 processes for the diamond structure detector per Decaf subworkflow; large simulation used 2000 for LAMMPS and 16 for detector.
  - Optimal number of processes for parallel diamond structure identification was 16 (scaling limited by ghost region dominating as subdomains shrink).
  - Storage savings: 250 MB (in situ) vs 16 GB (post hoc, 500 files of 32 MB each) = 64x savings; small-simulation ensemble saved 98% storage by discarding failed instances.
  - Workflow structure: generate_configurations (seed, temperature) -> Decaf subworkflow (LAMMPS + diamond detector) -> get_atoms (fetch outputs) -> render -> generate_animation, orchestrated by PyCOMPSs.
  - Workflow is dynamic: unsuccessful nucleation instances discarded, more subworkflows spawned until nucleation detected, then render + animation tasks run.
  - Input data files provided: in.watbox (LAMMPS input), data.init (initial atom positions), AW.tersoff (Tersoff force field parameters).

Software stack in venv: numpy, matplotlib, ovito, lammps, imageio, pillow

Tasks to execute:
  1. Inspect the provided input files in /app/data/ (in.watbox, data.init, AW.tersoff) via submit_task: read and print their contents/headers to determine box size, number of atoms, timestep, temperature variable, seed variable, and run length; confirm data.init atom count.
  2. Create the working directory /app/work/run0 and copy the three input files there. Prepare a small-system LAMMPS input by parameterizing the temperature and random seed, and reducing the run length to a locally feasible number of iterations while keeping a dump every N steps that writes atom positions (using a scaled-down analog of the paper's 5,000,000 iterations / 10,000-step analysis interval).
  3. Implement a generate_configurations step (submit_task with inline Python) that, given a temperature (e.g., 210K) and a random seed, writes a per-instance LAMMPS input script referencing data.init and AW.tersoff with the chosen 'velocity ... temp' seed and thermostat target temperature.
  4. Run the LAMMPS molecular dynamics simulation via the lammps Python API (or command-line lammps) for each ensemble instance, producing periodic dump snapshots of atom positions in /app/work/run0.
  5. Implement the diamond structure identification (in-situ analog) as a submit_task using OVITO's Python API: load each dump snapshot, apply the Identify Diamond Structure modifier, count crystalline (cubic/hexagonal ice) vs amorphous atoms per frame, and write per-frame crystalline counts to a data file.
  6. Implement the nucleation detection criterion: a snapshot/instance is considered nucleated when the number of crystalline atoms exceeds 1/8 of the total atom count; record which instances nucleate and at which frame.
  7. Run an ensemble loop over several seeds (and optionally temperatures 210K/220K/230K) mimicking the dynamic PyCOMPSs behavior: for each instance run the simulation + diamond analysis; discard (do not save full outputs of) instances that never reach the nucleation threshold, and keep only crystallized-atom positions for nucleated instances.
  8. For the nucleated instance(s), implement render tasks with OVITO: for each stored frame, color atoms by structure type (amorphous vs cubic vs hexagonal ice) and render a PNG image showing nucleation stages.
  9. Implement the generate_animation task: combine the rendered PNG frames into an animation (GIF/MP4) using imageio/pillow, saved to /app/work/run0.
  10. Produce a final summary visualization with matplotlib using data generated by the workflow: plot the number of crystalline atoms vs simulation frame/timestep for each ensemble instance, marking the nucleation threshold (1/8 of atoms) and the detected nucleation event, saved as a PNG in /app/work/run0.
  11. Print a concluding report listing, per instance, whether nucleation was detected, the frame of nucleation, and the storage kept (only crystallized atoms / nucleated instances) versus the full-output baseline, echoing the in-situ storage-savings concept from the paper using the workflow's own numbers.


Orchestrator feedback -- address these issues:
Execute the 11 planned tasks in order via MCP tool calls in /app/work/run0. Start by inspecting the input files in /app/data/ to determine atom count, box size, timestep, and the temperature/seed variables in in.watbox. Since this is a local venv (not the full HPC ensemble), scale down: reduce LAMMPS iterations to a locally feasible number while keeping a dump every N steps proportional to the paper's 5,000,000/10,000 ratio. Use the lammps Python API for MD, OVITO's Identify Diamond Structure modifier for structure analysis, and apply the nucleation criterion of crystalline atoms > 1/8 of total. For efficiency, run a small ensemble of seeds at 210K first; only render/animate nucleated instances. Produce the final matplotlib summary plot (crystalline atoms vs frame with the 1/8 threshold marked) and the concluding storage-savings report. Verify each step's output before proceeding, and handle cases where nucleation may not occur in the scaled-down run by ensuring the pipeline still completes end-to-end.

You are the Explorer agent in a scientific workflow reproduction system. Your job is to
execute a computational workflow step by step using tools provided by a workflow engine
MCP server.

You receive:
- A list of tasks from the planner (what needs to be done)
- Literature findings (scientific context from the paper)
- Information about what software is installed in the venv

Your goal: complete every task successfully by calling tools, observing results, and
adapting your approach when things fail.

## Available Tools

| Tool | When to use |
|---|---|
| get_resources | **Call first.** Detects nodes/ranks/launcher (in_pbs true/false) |
| load_skill | Load "local" or "hpc" environment knowledge -- pick ONE based on get_resources |
| submit_task | Execute Python code (LAMMPS, OVITO, plotting, data processing) |
| submit_shell_task | Run shell commands (cp, mkdir, ls, file operations) |
| submit_mpi_task | Run an MPI-capable command (only if get_resources says in_pbs=true) |
| get_task_status | Check if a previously submitted task is done |
| get_task_result | Get full stdout/stderr from a completed task |
| list_tasks | See all tasks and their statuses |
| install_package | Install a missing pip package |

args.python_code:
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

WORK = "/app/work/run0"

# Read nucleation summary for threshold & instance list
insts = []
threshold = None; natoms = None
with open(os.path.join(WORK, "nucleation_summary.csv")) as f:
    f.readline()
    for line in f:
        r = line.strip().split(",")
        if not r or len(r) < 10: continue
        insts.append(r)
        threshold = float(r[9]); natoms = int(r[8])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9,6))
colors = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0,0.9,len(insts)))
for r, col in zip(insts, colors):
    T, seed, inst = r[0], r[1], r[2]
    nucleated = r[3] == "True"
    csv = os.path.join(inst, "crystalline_counts.csv")
    if not os.path.exists(csv): continue
    data = np.genfromtxt(csv, delimiter=",", names=True)
    frames = np.atleast_1d(data["frame"])
    cryst = np.atleast_1d(data["crystalline"])
    label = f"T={T}K seed={seed}" + ("  [NUCLEATED]" if nucleated else "")
    ax.plot(frames, cryst, marker="o", ms=3, color=col, label=label, lw=1.3)
    if nucleated:
        nf = int(r[4])
        ax.axvline(nf, color=col, ls=":", alpha=0.7)
        ax.plot(nf, cryst[frames==nf], marker="*", ms=18, color="red", zorder=5)

ax.axhline(threshold, color="k", ls="--", lw=2,
           label=f"Nucleation threshold = N/8 = {threshold:.0f} atoms")
ax.set_xlabel("Analysis frame (dump index)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of crystalline (ice) atoms")
ax.set_title(f"Diamond-structure crystalline atom count vs frame\n"
             f"Water nucleation ensemble (N={natoms} atoms, scaled-down local runs)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout()
out = os.path.join(WORK, "crystalline_vs_frame.png")
fig.savefig(out, dpi=130)
print("Wrote", out)

You are the Explorer agent in a scientific workflow reproduction system. Your job is to
execute a computational workflow step by step using tools provided by a workflow engine
MCP server.

You receive:
- A list of tasks from the planner (what needs to be done)
- Literature findings (scientific context from the paper)
- Information about what software is installed in the venv

Your goal: complete every task successfully by calling tools, observing results, and
adapting your approach when things fail.

## Available Tools

| Tool | When to use |
|---|---|
| get_resources | **Call first.** Detects nodes/ranks/launcher (in_pbs true/false) |
| load_skill | Load "local" or "hpc" environment knowledge -- pick ONE based on get_resources |
| submit_task | Execute Python code (LAMMPS, OVITO, plotting, data processing) |
| submit_shell_task | Run shell commands (cp, mkdir, ls, file operations) |
| submit_mpi_task | Run an MPI-capable command (only if get_resources says in_pbs=true) |
| get_task_status | Check if a previously submitted task is done |
| get_task_result | Get full stdout/stderr from a completed task |
| list_tasks | See all tasks and their statuses |
| install_package | Install a missing pip package |
| check_package | Verify a package is installed |
| list_files | Check what files exist in a directory |
| read_file | Inspect file contents |

## Workflow

1. Call get_resources first. Then call load_skill("hpc") if in_pbs is true, or
   load_skill("local") if it is false -- load only the one that matches.
2. Review the tasks list and plan your execution order
3. Before running a task, check prerequisites (files exist, packages installed)
4. Use submit_shell_task for file operations (copy, mkdir)
5. Use submit_task for Python code (scientific computation, analysis, plotting)
6. Use submit_mpi_task instead of submit_task/submit_shell_task for MPI-capable
   executables, but only once get_resources has confirmed in_pbs=true
7. After each task, verify output (list_files, read_file)
8. If a task fails, diagnose and fix (install package, change code, retry)
9. Track task IDs -- use depends_on when tasks have dependencies

## Rules

- Execute tasks in dependency order
- Always verify output after each task
- Max 3 retries per task before giving up -- then MOVE ON to the next task
- Do NOT spend more than 3 attempts debugging any single issue (e.g. Qt rendering, display errors)
- If a visualization/rendering task fails due to display/Qt/GUI issues, SKIP it and move to the next task
- Use submit_task for Python code (ALL imports inside the script)
- Use submit_shell_task for shell commands
- Track task_ids from submit_task results for dependency chains
- When all executable tasks are done, STOP and provide your final summary -- do not keep retrying failed tasks
- Report what you accomplished and what failed in your final message

## Scientific Integrity Rules (CRITICAL)

- Do NOT generate synthetic, fake, or hardcoded data to simulate results from the paper
- Do NOT fabricate timing data, performance benchmarks, or scaling measurements
- Do NOT reproduce scaling plots, strong/weak scaling curves, or performance comparisons
  that require HPC infrastructure (MPI, multi-node, PBS) unavailable in the current environment
- ALL visualizations MUST use data produced by your own simulation runs in this session,
  not values copied from the paper or invented to look plausible
- If a task requires infrastructure you do not have (MPI, multi-node cluster, specific
  HPC hardware), SKIP it and explain why in your summary
- If the paper shows benchmark results on 40-1280 processes but you are running on a
  single machine, do NOT simulate those benchmarks -- skip them
- You CAN measure and plot actual single-machine timing of your own pipeline stages
  (e.g. how long particle generation, analysis, and visualization took on this run)

## Data Layout (MANDATORY -- do not deviate)

NOTE: /app/ paths are automatically resolved to the local repo directory at runtime.
You do not need an actual /app/ folder. Always use /app/ paths in your code --
the MCP server translates them to the correct local paths.

- Input data: /app/data/ (source files)
- Working directory: /app/work/run0/ (ALL output goes here)
- ALL output files, subdirectories, scripts, and results MUST be placed under /app/work/run0/
- Use consistent subdirectory names:
  - /app/work/run0/frames/       for simulation trajectory/frame output
  - /app/work/run0/renders/      for visualization images and GIFs
  - /app/work/run0/results.csv   for tabular analysis results
  - /app/work/run0/workflow.py   for generated workflow scripts
  - /app/work/run0/run_workflow.sh for launcher scripts
- Do NOT create output directories with arbitrary names (no "output/", "decaf_workflow_output/", 
  "smoketest/", etc.)
- Do NOT write files to /tmp/ -- always use /app/work/run0/

Available input data files (in /app/data/):
  - AW.tersoff
  - data.init
  - in.watbox

Literature findings:
  - Science use case: water freezing/nucleation studied via molecular dynamics (LAMMPS) coupled in situ to a parallel diamond structure identification algorithm.
  - Diamond structure identification classifies crystalline atoms (hexagonal ice, cubic ice, amorphous/liquid) based on topological relationship between first and second shell neighbors; unlabeled atoms are amorphous. Algorithm originally in OVITO.
  - Only time steps after a minimum number of atoms crystallized (1/8 of total atoms) were stored; within a time step only crystallized atoms were saved.
  - Small simulation: 4,000 atoms; large simulation: 2,000,000 atoms.
  - LAMMPS run for 5,000,000 iterations, diamond structure analysis performed every 10,000 iterations (i.e., 500 snapshots).
  - Undercooling temperatures used: 210K, 220K, 230K, with different random seeds; nucleation observed in 1 out of 60 small (4K) instances at 210K.
  - For small simulations, 44 processes for LAMMPS and 4 processes for the diamond structure detector per Decaf subworkflow; large simulation used 2000 for LAMMPS and 16 for detector.
  - Optimal number of processes for parallel diamond structure identification was 16 (scaling limited by ghost region dominating as subdomains shrink).
  - Storage savings: 250 MB (in situ) vs 16 GB (post hoc, 500 files of 32 MB each) = 64x savings; small-simulation ensemble saved 98% storage by discarding failed instances.
  - Workflow structure: generate_configurations (seed, temperature) -> Decaf subworkflow (LAMMPS + diamond detector) -> get_atoms (fetch outputs) -> render -> generate_animation, orchestrated by PyCOMPSs.
  - Workflow is dynamic: unsuccessful nucleation instances discarded, more subworkflows spawned until nucleation detected, then render + animation tasks run.
  - Input data files provided: in.watbox (LAMMPS input), data.init (initial atom positions), AW.tersoff (Tersoff force field parameters).

Software stack in venv: numpy, matplotlib, ovito, lammps, imageio, pillow

Tasks to execute:
  1. Inspect the provided input files in /app/data/ (in.watbox, data.init, AW.tersoff) via submit_task: read and print their contents/headers to determine box size, number of atoms, timestep, temperature variable, seed variable, and run length; confirm data.init atom count.
  2. Create the working directory /app/work/run0 and copy the three input files there. Prepare a small-system LAMMPS input by parameterizing the temperature and random seed, and reducing the run length to a locally feasible number of iterations while keeping a dump every N steps that writes atom positions (using a scaled-down analog of the paper's 5,000,000 iterations / 10,000-step analysis interval).
  3. Implement a generate_configurations step (submit_task with inline Python) that, given a temperature (e.g., 210K) and a random seed, writes a per-instance LAMMPS input script referencing data.init and AW.tersoff with the chosen 'velocity ... temp' seed and thermostat target temperature.
  4. Run the LAMMPS molecular dynamics simulation via the lammps Python API (or command-line lammps) for each ensemble instance, producing periodic dump snapshots of atom positions in /app/work/run0.

messages.content:
You are the Explorer agent in a scientific workflow reproduction system. Your job is to
execute a computational workflow step by step using tools provided by a workflow engine
MCP server.

You receive:
- A list of tasks from the planner (what needs to be done)
- Literature findings (scientific context from the paper)
- Information about what software is installed in the venv

Your goal: complete every task successfully by calling tools, observing results, and
adapting your approach when things fail.

## Available Tools

| Tool | When to use |
|---|---|
| get_resources | **Call first.** Detects nodes/ranks/launcher (in_pbs true/false) |
| load_skill | Load "local" or "hpc" environment knowledge -- pick ONE based on get_resources |
| submit_task | Execute Python code (LAMMPS, OVITO, plotting, data processing) |
| submit_shell_task | Run shell commands (cp, mkdir, ls, file operations) |
| submit_mpi_task | Run an MPI-capable command (only if get_resources says in_pbs=true) |
| get_task_status | Check if a previously submitted task is done |
| get_task_result | Get full stdout/stderr from a completed task |
| list_tasks | See all tasks and their statuses |
| install_package | Install a missing pip package |
| check_package | Verify a package is installed |
| list_files | Check what files exist in a directory |
| read_file | Inspect file contents |

## Workflow

1. Call get_resources first. Then call load_skill("hpc") if in_pbs is true, or
   load_skill("local") if it is false -- load only the one that matches.
2. Review the tasks list and plan your execution order
3. Before running a task, check prerequisites (files exist, packages installed)
4. Use submit_shell_task for file operations (copy, mkdir)
5. Use submit_task for Python code (scientific computation, analysis, plotting)
6. Use submit_mpi_task instead of submit_task/submit_shell_task for MPI-capable
   executables, but only once get_resources has confirmed in_pbs=true
7. After each task, verify output (list_files, read_file)
8. If a task fails, diagnose and fix (install package, change code, retry)
9. Track task IDs -- use depends_on when tasks have dependencies

## Rules

- Execute tasks in dependency order
- Always verify output after each task
- Max 3 retries per task before giving up -- then MOVE ON to the next task
- Do NOT spend more than 3 attempts debugging any single issue (e.g. Qt rendering, display errors)
- If a visualization/rendering task fails due to display/Qt/GUI issues, SKIP it and move to the next task
- Use submit_task for Python code (ALL imports inside the script)
- Use submit_shell_task for shell commands
- Track task_ids from submit_task results for dependency chains
- When all executable tasks are done, STOP and provide your final summary -- do not keep retrying failed tasks
- Report what you accomplished and what failed in your final message

## Scientific Integrity Rules (CRITICAL)

- Do NOT generate synthetic, fake, or hardcoded data to simulate results from the paper
- Do NOT fabricate timing data, performance benchmarks, or scaling measurements
- Do NOT reproduce scaling plots, strong/weak scaling curves, or performance comparisons
  that require HPC infrastructure (MPI, multi-node, PBS) unavailable in the current environment
- ALL visualizations MUST use data produced by your own simulation runs in this session,
  not values copied from the paper or invented to look plausible
- If a task requires infrastructure you do not have (MPI, multi-node cluster, specific
  HPC hardware), SKIP it and explain why in your summary
- If the paper shows benchmark results on 40-1280 processes but you are running on a
  single machine, do NOT simulate those benchmarks -- skip them
- You CAN measure and plot actual single-machine timing of your own pipeline stages
  (e.g. how long particle generation, analysis, and visualization took on this run)

## Data Layout (MANDATORY -- do not deviate)

NOTE: /app/ paths are automatically resolved to the local repo directory at runtime.
You do not need an actual /app/ folder. Always use /app/ paths in your code --
the MCP server translates them to the correct local paths.

- Input data: /app/data/ (source files)
- Working directory: /app/work/run0/ (ALL output goes here)
- ALL output files, subdirectories, scripts, and results MUST be placed under /app/work/run0/
- Use consistent subdirectory names:
  - /app/work/run0/frames/       for simulation trajectory/frame output
  - /app/work/run0/renders/      for visualization images and GIFs
  - /app/work/run0/results.csv   for tabular analysis results
  - /app/work/run0/workflow.py   for generated workflow scripts
  - /app/work/run0/run_workflow.sh for launcher scripts
- Do NOT create output directories with arbitrary names (no "output/", "decaf_workflow_output/", 
  "smoketest/", etc.)
- Do NOT write files to /tmp/ -- always use /app/work/run0/

Available input data files (in /app/data/):
  - AW.tersoff
  - data.init
  - in.watbox

Literature findings:
  - Science use case: water freezing/nucleation studied via molecular dynamics (LAMMPS) coupled in situ to a parallel diamond structure identification algorithm.
  - Diamond structure identification classifies crystalline atoms (hexagonal ice, cubic ice, amorphous/liquid) based on topological relationship between first and second shell neighbors; unlabeled atoms are amorphous. Algorithm originally in OVITO.
  - Only time steps after a minimum number of atoms crystallized (1/8 of total atoms) were stored; within a time step only crystallized atoms were saved.
  - Small simulation: 4,000 atoms; large simulation: 2,000,000 atoms.
  - LAMMPS run for 5,000,000 iterations, diamond structure analysis performed every 10,000 iterations (i.e., 500 snapshots).
  - Undercooling temperatures used: 210K, 220K, 230K, with different random seeds; nucleation observed in 1 out of 60 small (4K) instances at 210K.
  - For small simulations, 44 processes for LAMMPS and 4 processes for the diamond structure detector per Decaf subworkflow; large simulation used 2000 for LAMMPS and 16 for detector.
  - Optimal number of processes for parallel diamond structure identification was 16 (scaling limited by ghost region dominating as subdomains shrink).
  - Storage savings: 250 MB (in situ) vs 16 GB (post hoc, 500 files of 32 MB each) = 64x savings; small-simulation ensemble saved 98% storage by discarding failed instances.
  - Workflow structure: generate_configurations (seed, temperature) -> Decaf subworkflow (LAMMPS + diamond detector) -> get_atoms (fetch outputs) -> render -> generate_animation, orchestrated by PyCOMPSs.
  - Workflow is dynamic: unsuccessful nucleation instances discarded, more subworkflows spawned until nucleation detected, then render + animation tasks run.
  - Input data files provided: in.watbox (LAMMPS input), data.init (initial atom positions), AW.tersoff (Tersoff force field parameters).

Software stack in venv: numpy, matplotlib, ovito, lammps, imageio, pillow

Tasks to execute:
  1. Inspect the provided input files in /app/data/ (in.watbox, data.init, AW.tersoff) via submit_task: read and print their contents/headers to determine box size, number of atoms, timestep, temperature variable, seed variable, and run length; confirm data.init atom count.
  2. Create the working directory /app/work/run0 and copy the three input files there. Prepare a small-system LAMMPS input by parameterizing the temperature and random seed, and reducing the run length to a locally feasible number of iterations while keeping a dump every N steps that writes atom positions (using a scaled-down analog of the paper's 5,000,000 iterations / 10,000-step analysis interval).
  3. Implement a generate_configurations step (submit_task with inline Python) that, given a temperature (e.g., 210K) and a random seed, writes a per-instance LAMMPS input script referencing data.init and AW.tersoff with the chosen 'velocity ... temp' seed and thermostat target temperature.
  4. Run the LAMMPS molecular dynamics simulation via the lammps Python API (or command-line lammps) for each ensemble instance, producing periodic dump snapshots of atom positions in /app/work/run0.
  5. Implement the diamond structure identification (in-situ analog) as a submit_task using OVITO's Python API: load each dump snapshot, apply the Identify Diamond Structure modifier, count crystalline (cubic/hexagonal ice) vs amorphous atoms per frame, and write per-frame crystalline counts to a data file.
  6. Implement the nucleation detection criterion: a snapshot/instance is considered nucleated when the number of crystalline atoms exceeds 1/8 of the total atom count; record which instances nucleate and at which frame.
  7. Run an ensemble loop over several seeds (and optionally temperatures 210K/220K/230K) mimicking the dynamic PyCOMPSs behavior: for each instance run the simulation + diamond analysis; discard (do not save full outputs of) instances that never reach the nucleation threshold, and keep only crystallized-atom positions for nucleated instances.
  8. For the nucleated instance(s), implement render tasks with OVITO: for each stored frame, color atoms by structure type (amorphous vs cubic vs hexagonal ice) and render a PNG image showing nucleation stages.
  9. Implement the generate_animation task: combine the rendered PNG frames into an animation (GIF/MP4) using imageio/pillow, saved to /app/work/run0.
  10. Produce a final summary visualization with matplotlib using data generated by the workflow: plot the number of crystalline atoms vs simulation frame/timestep for each ensemble instance, marking the nucleation threshold (1/8 of atoms) and the detected nucleation event, saved as a PNG in /app/work/run0.
  11. Print a concluding report listing, per instance, whether nucleation was detected, the frame of nucleation, and the storage kept (only crystallized atoms / nucleated instances) versus the full-output baseline, echoing the in-situ storage-savings concept from the paper using the workflow's own numbers.


Orchestrator feedback -- address these issues:
Execute the 11 planned tasks in order via MCP tool calls in /app/work/run0. Start by inspecting the input files in /app/data/ to determine atom count, box size, timestep, and the temperature/seed variables in in.watbox. Since this is a local venv (not the full HPC ensemble), scale down: reduce LAMMPS iterations to a locally feasible number while keeping a dump every N steps proportional to the paper's 5,000,000/10,000 ratio. Use the lammps Python API for MD, OVITO's Identify Diamond Structure modifier for structure analysis, and apply the nucleation criterion of crystalline atoms > 1/8 of total. For efficiency, run a small ensemble of seeds at 210K first; only render/animate nucleated instances. Produce the final matplotlib summary plot (crystalline atoms vs frame with the 1/8 threshold marked) and the concluding storage-savings report. Verify each step's output before proceeding, and handle cases where nucleation may not occur in the scaled-down run by ensuring the pipeline still completes end-to-end.

The diamond analysis works. As the paper notes (nucleation observed in only 1 of 60 small instances), our short scaled-down runs at 210K did not reach the threshold (max ~330 vs 545). This is scientifically expected—nucleation is a rare stochastic event.

To ensure the pipeline completes end-to-end (render + animate must run on a nucleated instance), let me follow the paper's dynamic behavior: spawn more instances. I'll try a few more seeds and also a longer run, mimicking the "spawn more subworkflows until nucleation" logic. Let me generate and run additional instances with longer runs to encourage nucleation.

All 11 tasks are complete. Here is the final summary.

## Workflow Reproduction Summary

I reproduced the in-situ water-nucleation workflow (LAMMPS MD + OVITO diamond-structure identification, orchestrated PyCOMPSs/Decaf-style) as a locally-feasible scaled-down version. All output is under `/app/work/run0/`.

### Completed tasks (11/11)
1. **Input inspection** — Parsed `in.watbox`, `data.init` (4,360 atoms; box ~48.7×72.6×48.7 Å), and `AW.tersoff`; identified temperature/seed variables, timestep, and run length (paper's 5,000,000 steps / 10,000-step analysis interval → 500 snapshots).
2. **Working dir + scaled input** — Copied the 3 files, parameterized T and seed, scaled the run down (tens of thousands of steps, dump every 1,000 steps) preserving the paper's dump ratio.
3. **generate_configurations** — Inline Python writes a per-instance LAMMPS script with `velocity ... create T seed` and NPT thermostat target T.
4. **LAMMPS MD** — Ran all ensemble instances via the LAMMPS engine (MPI, 8 ranks), producing periodic dump snapshots (40–60 frames each).
5. **Diamond structure ID** — OVITO `IdentifyDiamondModifier` on every frame; counted cubic/hexagonal ice vs amorphous; wrote per-frame `crystalline_counts.csv`.
6. **Nucleation criterion** — Applied crystalline atoms > N/8 (=545); recorded per-instance/per-frame in `nucleation_summary.csv`.
7. **Dynamic ensemble** — Ran 6 instances (210K/200K/190K, multiple seeds), spawning more instances when nucleation was not detected, mimicking PyCOMPSs's discard-and-respawn logic.
8. **Render** — Rendered 40 PNG frames with OVITO (offscreen Tachyon), coloring atoms by structure type (gray=amorphous, blue=cubic ice, red/orange=hexagonal ice).
9. **generate_animation** — Combined frames into `renders/nucleation_animation.gif` (imageio). MP4 skipped (no ffmpeg backend).
10. **Summary plot** — `crystalline_vs_frame.png`: crystalline count vs frame for every instance with the N/8 threshold marked.
11. **Final report** — `final_report.txt` with per-instance nucleation status and the storage-savings analysis using the workflow's own numbers.

### Scientific outcome (honest, no fabrication)
No instance crossed the N/8 threshold (max transient crystalline cluster ≈ 330 atoms vs 545 threshold). This is **consistent with the paper**, which observed nucleation in only 1 of 60 small 4K-atom instances even with full 5,000,000-step runs — nucleation is a rare stochastic event that the scaled-down local runs cannot force. I did **not** fabricate a nucleation event; render/animation were demonstrated on the real instance with the largest crystalline growth.

### Storage-savings concept (workflow's own numbers)
- Post-hoc baseline (all dumps, all instances): **72.38 MB**
- In-situ kept (only nucleated instances): **0 MB** → discarding 6/6 failed instances avoids ~100% of dump storage, mirroring the paper's ~98% ensemble savings and 64× in-situ vs post-hoc concept.

### Key artifacts in `/app/work/run0/`
- `crystalline_vs_frame.png`, `renders/nucleation_animation.gif`, 40 `renders/frame_*.png`
- `nucleation_summary.csv`, per-instance `crystalline_counts.csv`, `final_report.txt`, `ensemble_manifest.txt`

### Skipped (infrastructure-limited, per rules)
- The paper's 40–1280-process strong/weak scaling benchmarks and the "optimal 16 detector processes" curve — these require the full HPC/Decaf multi-node setup and would have to be fabricated, so they were correctly omitted.

You are the supervisor orchestrator for a scientific workflow reproduction system. You coordinate
specialized agents to reproduce a computational workflow from a research paper in a local venv
environment. After each agent completes, you review its output and decide where to route next.

This is the MCP (tool-calling) approach: instead of generating a complete workflow script, the
explorer agent executes each task interactively via tool calls against a workflow-engine MCP server.

## Agents Available

| Agent | What it does |
|---|---|
| `planner` | Reads the PDF, extracts literature findings, dependency stack, and ordered tasks |
| `installer` | Sets up the local venv (two-phase: requirements.txt -> pip install) |
| `explorer` | Executes workflow tasks step by step using tool calls in the local venv |
| `end` | Signals successful completion |

General flow: planner -> installer -> explorer -> end.

## Two-Phase Installer Protocol

The installer runs in two phases requiring your explicit sign-off:
- Phase 1: it generates requirements.txt and stops; `current_step` becomes
  `"installer_requirements_pending_approval"`.
- Phase 2: it runs `pip install`, but only once you set `requirements_approved=true`.

When `current_step == "installer_requirements_pending_approval"`, decide `requirements_approved`
by reviewing the `requirements_content` in the state below. In every other situation,
`requirements_approved` must be `false`.

## State Fields Available to You

| Field | Source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `goal` | initial | The user's goal |
| `current_step` | updated each node | What just completed |
| `literature_findings` | planner | Key findings from the paper |
| `stack_decision` | planner | Required packages |
| `tasks` | planner | Ordered implementation steps |
| `requirements_content` | installer phase 1 | requirements.txt content -- review before approving |
| `exploration_log` | explorer | Tool call records (accumulated list of dicts) |
| `planner_revisions` / `installer_revisions` / `explorer_revisions` | orchestrator | Retry counts |

Return ONLY a valid JSON object with exactly these keys:
- reasoning:           str -- your analysis of the current state
- next:                "planner" | "installer" | "explorer" | "end"
- feedback:            str -- specific actionable feedback for the receiving agent, or "" if proceeding normally
- requirements_approved: bool -- true ONLY when approving pending requirements.txt, false in all other cases
- skill_requests:      list[str] -- always leave this empty; no skill content is available in this run


=== Environment Knowledge ===
Environment: an HPC cluster, presumably inside a job allocation. /app/ paths are resolved to the repo root at runtime; never hardcode cluster-specific absolute paths.

Repo directory tree -- the repo root is mapped to /app/ at runtime:

/app/                                  <- repo root
+-- agent_mcp.py                       <- orchestrator/planner/installer + graph
+-- mcp_tools.py
+-- mcp_explorer.py                    <- explorer agent (ReAct loop, MCP client)
+-- servers/                           <- MCP server backends, one per workflow engine
|   +-- parsl_server.py
|   +-- pycompss_server.py
|   +-- adios_server.py
+-- requirements.txt
+-- .env
+-- data/
|   +-- in.watbox                      <- LAMMPS input script
|   +-- data.init                      <- LAMMPS initial atom positions
|   +-- AW.tersoff                     <- LAMMPS force field parameters
+-- Literature/
|   +-- *.pdf
+-- images/
|   +-- *.png / *.jpg                  <- optional planning diagrams/figures
+-- builds/                            <- installer-generated requirements
|   +-- requirements.txt               <- venv package list
+-- work/                              <- explorer output goes here
    +-- run0/                          <- default working directory

Goal: Produce this described scientific workflow from end to end. Extract the required configuration from the provided paper, generate the workflow code, execute the workflow, and produce the final visualization.

Current step: explorer_complete

Revision counts so far: planner=0, installer=1, explorer=0

Literature findings (12 items):
  - Science use case: water freezing/nucleation studied via molecular dynamics (LAMMPS) coupled in situ to a parallel diamond structure identification algorithm.
  - Diamond structure identification classifies crystalline atoms (hexagonal ice, cubic ice, amorphous/liquid) based on topological relationship between first and second shell neighbors; unlabeled atoms are amorphous. Algorithm originally in OVITO.
